slides.heading: Move Element To End
slides.subtitle: AlgoExpert · Medium · Arrays
slides.narration: Let's solve Move Element To End, a medium arrays problem. We'll restate the problem, build the intuition, walk through the approach, read the Java solution, and finish with its complexity.

slides.heading: The problem
bullets: In place, move every occurrence of `toMove` to the end (other order irrelevant).
slides.narration: Here's the problem. In place, move every occurrence of toMove to the end (other order irrelevant).

slides.heading: Intuition
bullets: Two pointers: move the target from the left end out of the way by swapping with non-targets from the right.
slides.narration: Two pointers: move the target from the left end out of the way by swapping with non-targets from the right.

slides.heading: Brute force vs optimal
bullets: Build a new list: non-targets then targets → O(n) space
Bubble targets one step at a time → O(n²)
Two pointers in place → O(n), O(1) space
slides.narration: You could build a new list, or bubble each two to the end one step at a time, which is quadratic. Two pointers swap targets from the left with non-targets from the right in a single pass, in place.

slides.heading: Approach
bullets: 2. Skip targets already at the right
3. Swap a target on the left with a non-target on the right
slides.narration: Step by step. First, left and right pointers. Second, skip targets already at the right. Third, swap a target on the left with a non-target on the right. Fourth, meet in the middle.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: swap a[0] ↔ a[6]
slides.narration: The right pointer skips trailing twos and stops at index 6. The left value was a two, so we swap it to the right.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: a[1] = 1 ≠ 2, keep
slides.narration: The value at index 1 isn't a two, so it stays.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: swap a[2] ↔ a[5]
slides.narration: The right pointer skips trailing twos and stops at index 5. The left value was a two, so we swap it to the right.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: swap a[3] ↔ a[3]
slides.narration: The right pointer skips trailing twos and stops at index 3. The left value was a two, so we swap it to the right.

slides.heading: Java solution
slides.narration: While l is less than r, we move r left past targets, swap if the left element is the target, then advance l.

slides.heading: Complexity
slides.narration: Time is O of n. Space is constant.

slides.heading: Edge cases & pitfalls
bullets: Order of other elements need not be kept
Check l < r inside the inner loop
slides.narration: The problem doesn't require preserving order of the other elements. Guard the inner loop with l less than r so it never crosses.

slides.heading: Interview tips & follow-ups
bullets: Follow-up: keep relative order (stable) → write pointer
slides.narration: If order must be preserved, use a write pointer that copies non-targets forward, then fill the tail with targets.

slides.heading: Recap
bullets: Two pointers: move the target from the left end out of the way by swapping with non-targets from the right.
slides.narration: To recap Move Element To End: Two pointers: move the target from the left end out of the way by swapping with non-targets from the right. Try re-implementing it from scratch without looking.
